title: Disease and ectoparasite management improve nestling golden eagle health and survival: An effective mitigation strategy
abstract: Changes in the distribution and behavior of pathogens and parasites associated with climate change are creating emerging threats for wildlife. These threats have created an urgent need for conservation strategies to manage wildlife. Conservation strategies could provide reliable and cost-effective compensatory mitigation options for protected species affected by renewable energy production, such as golden eagles (Aquila chrysaetos). We used nest camera data to assess survival and cause of death for golden eagle nestlings in southern Idaho, USA. Together, poultry bugs (Haematosiphon inodorus), a blood-sucking ectoparasite that lives in golden eagle nests, and trichomonosis, a fatal disease that is transmitted through the consumption of rock pigeons (Columba livia) caused ~ 27% of nestlings to die per year. From 2022-2023, we treated trichomonosis-infected nestlings with an anti-protozoan drug and developed a protocol for reducing poultry bug densities in eagle nests, then we projected the effects of disease and parasite treatments on population growth using simulation models. We collected pre-treatment information on nestling health and survival, and then, after young fledged, we applied 1 of 3 experimental parasite treatments to eagle nests: permethrin and diatomaceous earth, diatomaceous earth only, or water - a control, and measured effects on eagle health and survival the following year. Ten eagle nestlings with trichomonosis, that otherwise would have died, were successfully treated and lived to fledge from the nest. The permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatment significantly reduced poultry bug densities in eagle nests in the subsequent breeding season and created measurable improvements to nestling health and survival. Nestlings had significantly higher hematocrit, female nestlings had higher mass, and, on average, more nestlings (0.70) successfully survived to fledge compared with control- and diatomaceous earth-treated nests. Further, treatment of disease and parasites was projected to increase population growth rates by 4% and 8%, respectively. In total, we estimate saving 17.5 nestlings, which equates to 10.2 adult eagles, through disease and parasite treatments in two years. In areas with dense concentrations of poultry bugs or where eagles consume rock pigeons, disease and parasite treatments could be an effective compensatory mitigation option or management tool with population-level impacts on eagle populations.

## 16 **Abstract**

- 17 Changes in the distribution and behavior of pathogens and parasites associated with climate

- 18 change are creating emerging threats for wildlife. These threats have created an urgent need for

- 19 conservation strategies to manage wildlife. Conservation strategies could provide reliable and

- 24 nests, and trichomonosis, a fatal disease that is transmitted through the consumption of rock

- 42 treatments could be an effective compensatory mitigation option or management tool with

- 43 population-level impacts on eagle populations.

- 44 **Introduction**

- 45 Climate change is altering the distribution and behavior of various pathogens and parasites,

- 46 leading to an increased risk for wildlife (Harvell et al., 2002). For example, rising temperatures

- 47 and changing precipitation patterns can expand the geographical range of disease vectors,

- 48 exposing wildlife populations to novel infections (Lafferty, 2009), or increase the overwinter

- 49 survival of parasites or vectors, leading to greater infection risk (Bale and Hayward, 2010,

- 50 although see Brown et al., 2022). Additionally, landscape changes might disrupt ecosystem

- 51 dynamics, making some species more susceptible to infections (Hassell et al., 2013). The

- 52 compounding effects of environmental change on disease dynamics underscore the urgency of

- 53 comprehensive conservation strategies to mitigate these threats to wildlife health, particularly for 54 species of conservation concern (Smith et al., 2006).

- 55 Apex avian predators (raptors) are declining worldwide (McClure et al., 2018) and they

- 56 are particularly susceptible to parasites and pathogens (Blanco et al., 2022; van den Brand et al.,

- 57 2015; Vidaña et al., 2020). Raptors often migrate long distances or have large home ranges,

- 58 which can increase exposure to pathogens (Altizer et al., 2011). Further, raptor nests are large

- 59 and provide optimal ectoparasite habitat (Philips and Dindal, 1977) and an easily accessible food

- 60 source (i.e., nestlings) that cannot leave the nest until fledging (Philips, 2007). Finally,

- 61 ecosystem changes in trophic systems can expose raptors to disease through novel interactions

- 62 with pathogens or vectors. For example, as the preferred prey of Bonelli’s eagles ( _Aquila_

- 63 _fasciata_ ) decreases, eagles switch prey to forage on rock pigeons ( _Columba livia_ ) that carry the

- 64 protozoan _Trichomonas gallinae,_ which can cause the disease trichomonosis and nestling death

- 65 (Palma et al., 2006; Real et al., 2000).

- 66 Golden eagles ( _Aquila chrysaetos_ ) in western North America are affected by disease and

- 67 parasites. Like Bonelli's eagles, when faced with habitat degradation and reduced availability of

- 68 preferred prey such as black-tailed jackrabbits ( _Lepus californicus_ ), golden eagles switch to

- 69 alternative prey such as rock pigeons the vectors of _T. gallinae_ that cause trichomonosis (Heath

- 70 et al., 2021). Trichomonosis is characterized by plaques in the oral cavity that grow to block the

- 71 esophagus and trachea of nestling eagles, resulting in a high mortality rate (Dudek et al., 2018).

- 72 Further, poultry bugs ( _Haematosiphon inodorus_ , also known as Mexican chicken bugs), are a

- 73 blood-sucking ectoparasite in the family Cimicidae and are closely related to bed bugs ( _Cimex_

- 74 spp.) and swallow bugs ( _Oeciacus vicarius_ ). The effects of poultry bugs on golden eagles have

- 75 been documented for several decades in the southwestern US (Grubb et al., 1986; Wilson and

- 76 Oliver, 1978). More recently, the incidence and negative effects of poultry bugs on golden eagle

- 77 populations have increased (Murphy et al., 2023), perhaps because warming winters (Møller et

- 78 al., 2013) have led to the rapid expansion of the poultry bugs’ range (McFadzen et al., 1996).

- 79 Consequently, poultry bugs might be considered an emerging threat to golden eagles in much of

- 80 their western range. Poultry bugs live in nest material and emerge to feed on the blood of

- 81 nestlings. Poultry bugs reduce golden eagle nestling mass, blood hematocrit, and telomere length

- 82 (all correlates of nesting health), increase corticosterone (a hormone associated with physiologic

- 83 stress), and increase the probability that nestlings fledge early (and die) or die in the nest (Dudek

- 84 et al., 2021). Young eagles that successfully survive to fledge from a nest with poultry bugs have

- 85 a low probability of survival in their first year (Murphy et al., 2023).

- 86 Treatments for pathogens and parasites vary in approach and efficacy. Trichomonosis can

- 87 be treated if the infection is discovered early when the plaques are small. One dose of an anti-

- 88 protozoan reverses the infection and nestlings survive. Unfortunately, effective treatment options

- 89 for poultry bugs remain unclear. Organically derived products such as diatomaceous earth

- 90 (Bennett et al., 2011; Dawson, 2004; Kochert pers comm.) and pyrethrins (Fessl et al., 2006;

- 91 Hanssen et al., 2013) have previously been used to treat ectoparasites, including some from the

- 92 family Cimicidae (swallow bugs and poultry bugs). Diatomaceous earth abrades the cuticle of

- 93 the parasite, causing it to desiccate (Koruni ć , 2013). Pyrethrins and the synthetic version,

- 94 permethrin, impact the nervous system by disrupting the sodium ion channel and paralyzing the

- 95 insect (Soderlund et al., 2002). Though widely used to treat nest parasites, pyrethroids

- 96 applications can have side effects on young birds (Larsen et al., 2004, López-Arrabé et al., 2014)

- 97 or their offspring (Bulgarella et al., 2020) and may contain dangerous additives (Hund et al.,

- 98 2015). The most effective timing and dosages for the use of these products as a treatment for

- 99 poultry bugs in eagle nests, while minimizing impacts to nestling eagles, remains uncertain.

- 100 Given the increasing threat of disease and parasites, and the consistent timing (breeding

- 101 season) and location (nest) of their effect, the treatment of disease and parasites may be an

- 102 excellent management tool or mitigation option. Several US laws, including the Bald and Golden

- 103 Eagle Protection Act (16 U.S.C. 669-668c), protect eagles by preventing ‘take’, the killing,

- 104 wounding, or harassment of birds. The United States Fish and Wildlife Service manages the

- 105 permitting for individuals or organizations that may incidentally or unavoidably take eagles

- 106 while conducting otherwise lawful activities. As part of the permitting process, permittees are

- 107 often required to offset their take through mitigation. The US has a growing dependence on

- 108 large-scale renewable energy; particularly wind power. Mortality of juvenile and adult golden

- 109 eagles due to collisions with wind turbines has been documented (Millsap et al., 2022), creating a

- 110 need to identify reliable direct or compensatory mitigation options. Unfortunately, few

- 111 mitigation techniques can quantifiably demonstrate a net positive impact on eagle populations

- 112 (Allison et al., 2017). Increasing the number of mitigation options will benefit renewable energy

- 113 permittees and eagle populations by focusing conservation efforts on removing sources of eagle

- 114 mortality. To date, the reduction of eagle mortality caused by nest ectoparasites or disease has

- 115 not been widely considered for offsetting incidental eagle take.

- 116 Our objective was to examine the effects of disease and parasites on golden eagle

- 117 nestlings in southern Idaho, USA where golden eagles reach some of the highest nesting

- 118 densities in North America. Further, we aimed to treat nestlings for trichomonosis and develop

- 119 an effective treatment option for poultry bugs that minimizes potential side effects to eagles. The

- 120 incidence of trichomonosis in golden eagle nestlings has increased in southern Idaho with ~ 41%

- 121 of nestlings exposed to _T. gallinae_ and 25% of nestlings developing lethal oral plaques (Dudek et

- 122 al., 2018). In the same study area, poultry bugs were reported in golden eagle nests as early as

- 123 the late 1960s (Hickman, 1968). More recently, Dudek et al. (2021) found the presence of

- 124 poultry bugs in golden eagle nests to be widespread, affecting 77% of eagle nests. The consistent

- 125 and high rate of poultry bug infection of nests in southern Idaho provides an excellent

- 126 opportunity to test the efficacy of anti-parasite treatments on poultry bug presence and

- 127 abundance and nestling health and survival. We aimed to assess the efficacy of poultry bug

- 128 treatment strategies by testing two readily available anti-parasite products (diatomaceous earth

- 129 and permethrin) on nests of golden eagles in southern Idaho. Then, we projected whether

- 130 trichomonosis or poultry bug treatment could have population-level effects. Finally, we

- 131 considered whether nestling parasite and disease treatment may be a viable compensatory

- 132 mitigation option for golden eagle incidental take permittees.

- 133

- 134 **Methods**

- 135 Our study area was located in southwestern Idaho along the Snake River Canyon in the Morley

- 136 Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey National Conservation Area and surrounding areas (Figure 1).

- 137 Steep basalt cliffs in the Snake River Canyon and rocky outcrops provide ample sites for golden

- 138 eagles to construct large stick nests. The surrounding uplands consist of native shrub-steppe and

- 139 salt-desert communities characterized by sagebrush-dominated shrublands, native perennial

- 140 grasses, disturbed grasslands, rangeland dominated by exotic annual grasses, irrigated

- 141 agricultural land, and rural and suburban development (U.S. Department of the Interior, 1996).

- 142

- 143 _Effects of disease and parasites on nestling health_ . We monitored 80 – 90 historical golden

- 144 eagle nesting territories in southern Idaho in 2014 – 2015, 2017 – 2018, and 2021. We followed

- 145 ground-based survey methods described by Steenhof et al. (1997) to determine territory

- 146 occupancy and nesting attempts. Once we identified a nesting attempt, we made regular nest

- 147 observations from >400 meters to monitor outcomes and visually assess nestling age based on

- 148 feather development (Driscoll, 2010). We rappelled into 15 – 25 nests per year to install trail

- 149 cameras (Harrison et al., 2019) when nestlings were 2 – 3 weeks old and able to thermoregulate

- 150 (Katzner et al., 2020). Trail cameras were set to record images with either a motion-activated

- 151 trigger or a time-lapse setting of 1 image per hour. Once we did not observe young in the nest,

- 152 we returned to collect the cameras and review images.  We used camera images to determine the 153 date and age that nestlings fledged (left the nest) or died.

- 154 The cause of death was based on images and information we collected while visiting the

- 155 nest. When we installed cameras, we examined nestling eagles for trichomonosis plaques by

- 156 visually inspecting the sides of the mouth, oropharynx, and upper and lower surfaces of the

- 157 tongue. If we detected a possible lesion, we used a cotton swab to probe the lesion to test

- 158 whether it was attached or mobile (e.g., a piece of food). We considered immobile, caseous

- 159 lesions to be indicative of trichomonosis. If nestlings had trichomonosis, we treated individuals

- 160 with anti-protozoan medication (see below). Additionally, during our nest visit, we recorded

- 161 whether there were poultry bugs in the nest. We considered the cause of death to be

- 162 trichomonosis if a nestling had plaques in its mouth (treated or not). We considered the cause of

- 163 death to be poultry bugs if a nest was infested and a nestling died of starvation (despite prey

- 164 deliveries), or if a nestling jumped from an infested nest to its death before it could fly.

- 165

- 166 _Disease and Parasite Treatment._ Our study of disease and parasite treatments occurred in the

- 167 breeding seasons of 2021 – 2023. During all visits to nests with nestling eagles, we examined

- 168 nestling eagles for trichomonosis plaques as described above. Nestlings with caseous lesions

- 169 were treated with a 30 mg oral dose of carnidazole (Spartrix, Harkers, Suffolk, UK), an

- 170 antiprotozoal drug, to reduce the growth of plaques that would otherwise lead to nestling death.

- 171 The carnidazole was administered orally, by placing the tablet in the back of the esophagus so it 172 was swallowed. We followed the fate of these nestlings with camera images (see below).

- 173 Before parasite treatments, in 2021, we selected 18 occupied eagle territories with nesting

- 174 attempts for our pre-treatment assessment of poultry bugs. We visited nests when eagle nestlings

- 175 were ~ 3 weeks old, to bury 2 – 3 SenSci ActivVolcano Bed Bug Detector® (SenSci,

- 176 Lawrenceville, NJ, USA) traps within eagle nests. These small pitfall traps had a scent lure

- 177 designed to attract (from < 1 m) and capture common bed bugs ( _Cimex lectularius_ ), a closely

- 178 related species to poultry bugs. Traps were covered with a small cardboard ‘tent’ to prevent nest

- 179 material from falling into the trap. We took photographs and mapped the locations of the traps to

- 180 aid in the recovery of traps during the next visit. We returned to the nests again ~ 2 months later,

- 181 once the nests were empty, to retrieve the traps (and apply treatments, see below). We placed

- 182 recovered traps in sealable plastic bags and stored them in the freezer until the end of the season

- 183 when we tabulated trap contents.

- 184 We randomly assigned an equal number of territories to one of three treatment options: 1)

- 185 diatomaceous earth, 2) a combination of diatomaceous earth and permethrin (Permacap, BASF,

- 186 NJ, USA), or 3) a water-only (control) treatment. We considered eagle territories to be the

- 187 experimental units for our study of parasite treatments. Golden eagle nesting territories often

- 188 contain multiple alternative nests (Millsap et al., 2015). In southern Idaho, the number of nests

- 189 per territory can range from 1 to 18 with some pairs using the same nest every year, whereas

- 190 other pairs switch nests within their territory from year to year (Kochert and Steenhof, 2012). We

- 191 aimed to treat the three most recently used, and climber-accessible, nests within a territory. By

- 192 selecting multiple, recently used nests we increased the probability that the eagle pair would use

- 193 the treated nest in the subsequent breeding season (see below, Kochert and Steenhof, 2012;

- 194 Wiens et al., 2018). Further, adult eagles regularly perch on alternate nests and may act as

- 195 vectors by carrying poultry bugs from one nest to another. By treating several nests, we aimed to

- 196 decrease territory-level poultry bug load.

- 197 We applied all parasite treatments in the summer (mid-June – July) after the young had

- 198 fledged. By waiting until the young left the nest, we decreased researcher disturbance and

- 199 avoided potential secondary effects on nestling eagles from the treatments (López-Arrabé et al.,

- 200 2014). Despite nestlings eagles being out of the nest, the poultry bugs reside in eagle nests year-

- 201 round and remain active through the fall, leaving them vulnerable to treatment (Heath unpub.

- 202 data). We anticipated that a summer treatment would decrease annual poultry bug survival,

- 203 leading to a lower density of poultry bugs in eagle nests in subsequent springs. Diatomaceous

- 204 earth powder was dusted over the surface of the nest continuously, resulting in approximately 60

- 205 grams of treatment product being applied per nest (Dawson, 2004; Hanssen et al., 2013). Fluid-

- 206 based treatments (permethrin and water) were applied via a hand-pumped garden sprayer at a

- 207 rate of ~ 290 ml per square meter. Permacap was diluted to 1:10 before application. The crew

- 208 wore personal protective equipment including gloves, eye protection, and a respirator, when

- 209 applying all treatments. The treatment applied to each territory was randomly selected and

- 210 usually varied between years. Six territories were treated in only a single year, and 18 territories

- 211 were treated in both years, though not always with the same treatment. In some cases, treated

- 212 territories were not occupied in subsequent years, pairs did not attempt to breed, or nests were

- 213 inaccessible for climbing. At these territories, we were not able to collect post-treatment data on 214 either parasite load in the nest, nestling health, or both.

- 215 In 2022 and 2023, we monitored focal eagle territories in late winter and early spring (Jan

- 216 – Mar) for occupancy and observation of incubating eagles. We aimed to visit treated territories

- 217 when the young were approximately 21 days old and again when they were 45 – 56 days old (6.5

- 218 –  8 weeks). On the first nest visit, we placed SenSci ActivVolcano Bed Bug Detector® traps in

- 219 nests as described above and installed a nest camera to record nestling fate. On the second visit,

- 220 we recorded morphometric measurements, including mass (a measure of condition) and footpad

- 221 length (a size measure that can be used to determine nestling sex), and used a 25-gauge needle

- 222 and syringe to withdraw < 1 ml blood from the brachial vein to measure nestling hematocrit.

- 223 Finally, we returned to the nests to collect the traps and camera once all the young in the nest

- 224 were gone. We reviewed images from nest cameras to determine whether or not nestlings

- 225 successfully survived to fledge.

- 226

- 227 _Data synthesis and analysis_ . We estimated the effects of treatment for trichomonosis using an

- 228 intercept-only Poisson generalized linear mixed model (GLMM) with the number of nestlings

- 229 surviving to fledge per nest (hereafter nestling survivorship, Heath et al. 2021) as the response

- 230 variable. This model included data from all focal nests, even where trichomonosis was not

- 231 detected (i.e., treatment survivorship = 0), to estimate the effects of treatment study-wide. The

- 232 result is thus the number of fledglings produced by the treatment per visited nest. We included

- 233 territory identity as a random effect because some territories were sampled in more than one 234 year. We considered the effect to be statistically significant if the intercept was significantly

- 235 different from zero. We estimated “control” survivorship for the trichomonosis treatment using

- 236 the same model except that the dependent variable was the number of offspring that would have

- 237 fledged without treatment, i.e., the actual number that fledged minus the number treated. In both

- 238 models, the year and the number of visits per territory did not affect the number of young that 239 survived to fledging and these terms were removed.

- 240 We tallied all of the poultry bugs collected per nest. We used a GLMM with a negative

- 241 binomial distribution to examine whether period (pre- or post-treatment), treatment, or the

- 242 interaction between period and treatment explained poultry bug counts. This model included an

- 243 offset for the number of traps retrieved from each nest and a random effect of territory identity

- 244 because some territories were sampled in more than one year. We used general linear mixed

- 245 models to examine whether treatment affected nestling hematocrit or mass. We used sex as a

- 246 covariate for the mass model because female eagles are larger than male eagles. Both

- 247 morphometric models had a random effect for each nest event identity to account for data

- 248 collected from siblings.

- 249 We used a GLMM with a Poisson distribution to examine the effect of parasite treatment

- 250 on nestling survivorship. This model included a fixed effect of parasite treatment type and

- 251 random effects of year (categorical) and territory identity. For all analyses, we used a one-tailed

- 252 null hypothesis, with the alternative hypothesis that more young survived to fledge in treated

- 253 nests compared to controls. The one-tailed approach was used because we predicted that parasite

- 254 and disease treatment would only increase nestling survivorship and health and to decrease the

- 255 probability of a type II error given the relatively small sample sizes and possible small effect

- 256 sizes (i.e., eagle broods range from 0 – 3 young).

- 257

- 258 _Population Effects._ To inform potential mitigation strategies involving the mortality of golden

- 259 eagles from wind turbine collisions, we used previously published rates of survival (Millsap et al.

- 260 2022) and our nest survivorship estimates with simulations to project the relative number of adult 261 golden eagles and population growth rates produced by rescuing nestlings from disease and

- 262 parasites. We used nestling survivorship as a proxy for fecundity, though this estimate is biased 263 high because it does not include the fates of breeding attempts that failed early (i.e., < 3-week-

- 264 old nestling), before we were able to install a camera in the nest. However, the nestling

- 265 survivorship estimates are reasonable for comparing the relative effect size for disease and

- 266 parasite treatments – effects that occurred once young were older than 3 weeks. We estimated 267 nestling survivorship with and without disease and parasite treatments using the Poisson

- 268 GLMMs described above. These models produced mean estimates of nestling survivorship on

- 269 the log scale and their standard errors for treatment and control groups. We estimated fecundity, 270 the number of female young produced per female, as nestling survivorship divided by 2 thereby 271 assuming an approximately equal sex ratio.

- 272 We used simulation to examine the effects of our disease and parasite treatments on the 273 projected population growth rate (Lambda, λ ). We implemented simulations using the four-stage

- 274 Lefkovitch matrix from Millsap et al (2022) to examine population dynamics of golden eagles

- 275 across North America. We parameterized this matrix using survival rates estimated by Millsap et

- 276 al. (2022) and fecundity rates either with or without disease treatment or parasite treatment. We

- 277 modified code provided by Schaub and Kéry (2022; page 85) to randomly sample 10,000

- 278 survival values from a beta distribution, given average values of survival and their standard

- 279 errors.

- 280 Using model-estimated values of fecundity, we randomly drew 10,000 times from a

- 281 normal distribution as the mean and standard deviation on the log scale. Next, we exponentiated

- 282 these values to backtransform and divided them by two to obtain random draws of fecundity (i.e.,

- 283 female only). We first projected the effects of trichomonosis treatment on λ . We used the mean

- 284 and standard error of the control level of fecundity on the log scale outputted from the GLMM 285 described above and randomly drew 10,000 times from a normal distribution. Then, to estimate

- 286 the level of fecundity under the treatment regime, we added 10,000 draws of the effect size to the

- 287 draws of the control level of fecundity. We exponentiated these values and divided them by two 288 to obtain random draws of fecundity and parameterized 20,000 Lefkovitch matrices using these

- 289 draws of fecundity either with or without treatment and Millsap et al.’s (2022) survival estimates.

- 290 We performed a similar procedure to project the effects of treatment for poultry bugs on λ . We

- 291 again parameterized 20,000 Lefkovitch matrices using these draws of fecundity either with

- 292 (10,000 draws) or without (10,000 draws) parasite treatment, along with the random draws of

- 293 survival mentioned above.

294 We used these random draws of vital rates to project the number of adult golden eagles

- 295 resulting from our treatments. For each set of draws, we calculated the increase in fecundity

- 296 because of disease or parasite treatment then multiplied it by two to calculate the number of

- 297 offspring fledged (male and female). We then multiplied this value by each of the draws of first-,

- 298 second-, and third-year survival. This produced the number of adult eagles (age ≥ 3) resulting

- 299 from each territory treated. To estimate the number of adult eagles resulting from trichomonosis

- 300 treatment, we multiplied this value by the number of territories checked for trichomonosis (27).

- 301 To project the number of adult eagles resulting from parasite treatment, we multiplied the

- 302 number of adult eagles resulting per territory by the number of territories treated for parasites

- 303 (10). Our simulations yielded 10,000 values of λ and the number of adults resulting from

- 304 treatment. We added these draws of number of adult eagles together to determine the number of

- 305 adult eagles resulting from both treatments. We used the means, 5[th] , and 95[th] percentiles to

- 306 describe the central tendency and precision of these distributions.

- 307

- 308 **Results**

- 309 _Effects of disease and parasites on nestlings_ . We installed cameras in 56 nests across 33

- 310 territories from 2014 – 2015, 2017 – 2018, and 2021. We monitored the fate of 87 nestlings in

- 311 these 56 nests. Thirty-four of 87 nestlings (39%) died between 3 weeks old and fledging. The

- 312 most common causes of death were poultry bugs (35%), and trichomonosis (35%). In some

- 313 cases, nestlings had both poultry bugs and trichomonosis (6%). In total, 76% of deaths were

- 314 caused by parasites, disease, or both. There were some unknown causes of death (n = 6, 18%),

- 315 one nestling died from siblicide, and another of infanticide (6% combined).

- 316

- 317 _Disease and Parasite Treatments._ We examined 69 nestlings (2022 n = 28, 2023 n = 41) at 27

- 318 nests for trichomonosis and detected plaques in 12 nestlings (2022 n = 5, 2023 n = 7). We

- 319 successfully treated 10 eagle nestlings for trichomonosis and these individuals fledged. In two

- 320 other cases, we discovered the disease at a late stage, when the birds had large plaques. Although

- 321 we treated these birds, they did not survive because the disease was too progressed. On average,

- 322 nestling survivorship significantly increased by 0.37 nestlings per nest (90% CI: 0.22 **—** 0.62) 323 because of trichomonosis treatment.

- 324 We treated 14 territories (34 nests) with permethrin and diatomaceous earth (2021 n = 7,

- 325 2022 n = 7), 13 territories (35 nests) with diatomaceous earth (2021 n = 7, 2022 n = 6), and 15

- 326 territories (40 nests) served as controls (2021 n = 8, 2022 n = 7). In some nests, adult eagles 327 turned poultry bug pitfall traps over or removed them from the nest and they could not be

- 328 sampled. Therefore, our post-treatment sample size for poultry bug traps included 8 permethrin

- 329 and diatomaceous earth territories, 4 diatomaceous earth territories, and 6 control territories.

- 330 Poultry bug loads were similar across all groups in the pre-treatment period. We found a

- 331 significant interaction between treatment type and period on poultry bug loads. Permethrin and

- 332 diatomaceous earth treatment significantly decreased the poultry bug load in the post-treatment

- 333 period ( β pre*permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatment = 5.1 ± 1.6, z = 3.2, p < 0.01, Figure 2), but there was

- 334 no effect of treatment on post-treatment poultry bug loads in the diatomaceous earth ( β pre*

- 335 diatomaceous earth treatment[ = 1.7 ± 1.7, z = 1.0, p = 0.16, Figure 2) or control groups (][β] pre* control[ = 0.4 ± ]

- 336 0.8, z = 0.5, p = 0.31, Figure 2). Specifically, there were no highly infested nests in the

- 337 permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatment group, which greatly lowered the variance (Figure

- 338 2A) and the overall mean (Figure 2B) poultry bug load. We combined the diatomaceous earth

- 339 and control treatment groups into the control group for comparisons to the permethrin and

- 340 diatomaceous earth treatment in analyses of nestling health and survival because there were no

- 341 significant differences between the diatomaceous earth and control groups on poultry bug load. 342 We found that eagle nestlings in the permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatment group

- 343 had significantly higher hematocrit levels than nestling eagles from the control group ( β treatment =

- 344 5.8 ± 2.7, χ[2] = 4.7, p = 0.02, Figure 3). Further, female nestling eagles had significantly higher

- 345 mass than female nestlings from the control group ( β treatment = 686 ± 254, t = 2.7, p = 0.03, Figure

- 346 4). There was no effect of treatment on male mass ( β treatment = 178 ± 214, t = 0.83, p = 0.42,

- 347 Figure 4). Finally, more nestlings successfully fledged from nests that had been treated with

- 348 permethrin and diatomaceous earth compared to the control group ( β treatment = 0.76 ± 0.4, χ[2] =3.4,

- 349 p = 0.03, Figure 5). On average, 0.70 (90% CI: 0.18 — 1.22) more nestlings successfully fledged

- 350 from nests in permethrin and diatomaceous earth-treated territories (1.30 nestlings per nest, 90%

- 351 CI: 0.82 — 2.05) compared with control group territories (0.61 nestlings per nest, 90% CI: 0.37 352 — 1.00).

- 353

- 354 _Population Effects._ We estimated λ with no trichomonosis treatment to be 1.14 (90% CI: 1.09—

- 355 1.19) and with trichomonosis treatment to be 1.18 (90% CI: 1.13—1.24), a difference of 0.04

- 356 (90% CI: -0.01— 0.10; Figure 6). The number of adult eagles potentially added from

- 357 trichomonosis treatments was 0.23 (90% CI: 0.13 — 0.36) per treated territory and a total of 6.13

- 358 (90% CI: 3.45 — 9.90) within the 27 territories checked for trichomonosis.

- 359 We estimated λ with no parasite treatment to be 1.08 (90% CI: 1.02 — 1.14) and with

- 360 permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatments to be 1.17 (90% CI: 1.10 — 1.24), a difference of

- 361 0.09 (90% CI: 0.01 — 0.17; Figure 6). The number of additional adult eagles resulting from

- 362 parasite treatments was 0.41 (90% CI: 0.12 — 0.70) per treated territory and a total of 4.09 (90%

- 363 CI: 1.18 — 7.08) for the 10 treated territories with nesting eagles (Figure 7). In sum, we estimate

- 364 saving 17.51 (90% CI: 10.50— 25.47) nestlings which equates to 10.24 (90% CI: 6.12— 15.04)

- 365 adult eagles through disease and parasite treatments.

## 366

## 367 **Discussion**

- 368 Trichomonosis and poultry bugs were a substantial threat to golden eagle nestling

- 369 survivorship. We successfully treated most nestlings infected with trichomonosis with one dose

- 370 of an anti-protozoan drug. The permethrin and diatomaceous earth treatment significantly

- 371 reduced parasite loads in nests and these reductions improved nestling health. Specifically,

- 372 nestlings were less anemic, female nestlings had higher mass, and nestling survivorship was

- 373 higher. The parasite treatment, combined with disease treatments, resulted in 17.5 golden eagle

- 374 nestlings surviving to fledge that otherwise would have died. This equates to an additional 10.2

- 375 adult eagles in the population. Given the high certainty of threat locations, treatment success, and

- 376 the quantifiable nature of treatment, managing disease and parasite threats for golden eagles is an 377 excellent mitigation option.

- 378 We found that the majority of nestling deaths (76%) were attributable to disease and

- 379 parasites. This level of mortality significantly reduced fecundity and had consequences for

- 380 population growth (see below). The prevalence of trichomonosis among eagle nestlings was

- 381 high, but this disease was highly treatable with just one dose of an anti-protozoan drug if we

- 382 caught it early, before plaques were large. A high rate of trichomonosis can be attributed to eagle

- 383 consumption of rock pigeons, in the absence of black-tailed jackrabbits, their preferred prey, or

- 384 other suitable prey (Heath et al., 2021); underscoring the ecological repercussions of declining

- 385 prey populations and trophic cascades. The elimination of this threat would require restoring

- 386 shrub systems and associated herbivores, like jackrabbits, or removing rock pigeons so they are

- 387 no longer a vector. Both of these options are challenging, protracted, and expensive. Dependence

- 388 on alternative food sources, while indicative of the eagles' adaptability, could pose a significant

- 389 conservation challenge. If regional reliance on rock pigeons persists, it could potentially lead to

- 390 the establishment of a conservation-reliant population, wherein ongoing human intervention is

- 391 required to sustain their reproductive success. Poultry bugs are similarly challenging to manage

- 392 because these parasites are not host-specific. Nests of other bird species on the same cliffs or

- 393 rocky outcrops as eagles may become infested and may act as vectors or reservoirs for the

- 394 poultry bugs (McFadzen and Marzluff 1996). Therefore, the management of disease and parasite 395 threats will likely require repeatable, long-term strategies.

- 396 We significantly decreased poultry bug loads in eagle territories with permethrin and

- 397 diatomaceous earth, which had significant, positive effects on eagle nestling health and survival. 398 Poultry bug loads in eagle nests have increased in recent years likely because of higher

- 399 overwinter survival of poultry bugs with warming winters (Brown and Brown, 1986). We 400 reduced numbers of poultry bugs before overwintering by applying treatments after eagles left

- 401 the nest. Post-breeding treatment decreased the chance of long-term side effects on nestlings

- 402 from permethrin (Bulgarella et al., 2020) because Permacap is estimated to last 90 days and is

- 403 unlikely to affect eagles in subsequent seasons. However, how the application affects other

- 404 arthropods in the nests or other animals that use eagle nest structures (e.g., other birds and 405 snakes) should be considered.

- 406 There are several remaining questions to address to fine-tune the treatment of poultry

- 407 bugs in eagle nests. We applied permethrin with diatomaceous earth to increase insect

- 408 susceptibility to the neurotoxin, because diatomaceous earth scratches exoskeletons. However, it 409 is unclear if the combination is needed or whether permethrin could be effectively applied alone. 410 Diatomaceous earth applied on its own did not affect poultry bug load. Unlike permethrin, which 411 degrades, diatomaceous earth can persist in nests long term. Future research should compare the

- 412 efficacy of permethrin on its own with permethrin combined with diatomaceous earth. Further,

- 413 given that poultry bugs can live in other species' nests and disperse across nest substrates (Heath

- 414 unpub dat), it is unclear how often territories need to be treated to reduce poultry bug loads.

- 415 Research to investigate how often territories should be treated is important. Finally, rappelling

- 416 into eagle nests brings potential harm to the nest structures and the crew. Future work to use

- 417 uncrewed aerial vehicles to provide remote applications may be a safe and effective alternative. 418 Eagle health improved after parasite removal. Given the strong effects of poultry bugs on

- 419 eagle health (Dudek et al., 2021), this result is not surprising. Lower prey quality in recent years 420 (Heath et al., 2021) might make it more difficult for eagles to compensate for the energetic

- 421 demands of coping with parasites. Nestlings in treated nests had higher hematocrit, were less

- 422 anemic, and female nestlings were heavier compared to nestlings from control nests. It was

- 423 interesting that only female mass increased after treatment and not males. However, this result is

- 424 consistent with other studies of parasite removal that found sex-specific responses (Wolf et al.,

- 425 2023). Female eagles are larger than male eagles and must grow larger than males during the 426 nestling stage. Therefore, females may have a stronger response to the relaxed pressure of

- 427 parasitism. Indeed, we found sex-specific responses of eagle nestlings to parasitism in previous

- 428 work. Specifically, female telomeres but not male telomeres were shorter in parasitized nests 429 (Dudek et al., 2021).

- 430 In addition to improved health, nestling eagles had higher survivorship in permethrin and

- 431 diatomaceous earth-treated nests. This effect is probably because nestlings with high parasite

- 432 loads jump early from the nest and die, or they die from anemia and starvation (Dudek et al.,

- 433 2021). A recent paper by Murphy et al. (2023) showed that even if nestling eagles survived

- 434 parasitized nests long enough to fledge, many of them die in their first year, presumably because

- 435 they are in poor condition. Our unpublished data tracking juvenile eagles supports this

- 436 hypothesis. Consequently, the positive effect of parasite treatment on eagle survivorship is likely

- 437 to be even greater than what we documented by studying survival to fledging, and not longer.

- 438 Disease and parasite treatments had projected population-level consequences for golden

- 439 eagles. This result was surprising because the population viability of long-lived birds, like golden

- 440 eagles, is most sensitive to changes in adult survival. However, in this population, parasites and

- 441 disease caused 76% of the deaths of nestlings, and a high proportion (39%) of all nestlings died.

- 442 Projected population growth rates increased by 4% from trichomonosis treatment and 8% from

- 443 poultry bug treatment. The projected disease and parasite effects on λ were greater than the

- 444 estimated population-level effect of lead (0.8%, Slabe et al., 2022), a commonly cited threat to

- 445 eagles. In combination, poultry bug parasite and trichomonosis disease treatments resulted in

- 446 17.5 golden eagle nestlings surviving to fledge over two years that likely would have died

- 447 without this direct management intervention. Combined, these interventions could be used to 448 offset the take of 10.2 adult eagles.

- 449 The expansion of alternative energy infrastructure, habitat fragmentation, declining prey

- 450 bases, lead exposure, and vehicle collisions threaten eagles across their range and cause additive

- 451 mortality within populations (e.g., Heath et al., 2021; Katzner et al., 2012; Knick and Dyer 1997,

- 452 Murphy et al. 2023). Determining how to counteract these threats by off-setting eagle take is a

- 453 high priority. Further, parasites and disease threats are likely to worsen with climate change and

- 454 habitat degradation. Treating parasites and disease is an effective compensatory mitigation

- 455 option because it has population-level effects, while being reliable, cost-effective, and

- 456 quantifiable. Further, disease and parasite treatments impact populations faster than other

- 457 management options (i.e., habitat restoration). Given the high effectiveness of disease and

- 458 parasite treatments, and the easily documented positive effect that these treatments have on eagle

- 459 nestling survival, combined disease and parasite treatment for golden eagles seems like an

- 460 excellent option for management to increase population size and to offset take of adult eagles

- 461 resulting from the expansion of renewable energy infrastructure in the western United States.
